summary: Research a post-crash EV battery assessment service paid for by insurers: how it is done today, what insurers could save, competitors, Baltic market, legal and safety issues, and fit with our battery take-back chain

findings.angle: A: How post-crash EV battery assessment is done today (guidelines, procedures, checks, durations, costs, vendors). Researched 31 Oct 2026 with about 30 searches (EN/DE/NO/SV/NL/LV) and about 20 page or PDF fetches.
findings.summary: Today's post-crash EV battery assessment is mostly a safety-triage and paperwork process, not a measurement of battery health. The best primary document is the Swiss SVV/ASS/LiBaService24 annex "Analyse von HV-Batterien" (v9, signed 31 Oct 2025, published Mar 2026). It prescribes a non-destructive process: review of the accident event, visual inspection of the pack casing and underbody, then a BMS/OBD data read-out (fault codes, SoC, cell and module voltages and temperatures, insulation values, SoH, pyrofuse status). It sets hard exclusion rules: casing deformation of 10 mm or more in depth, a torn or holed casing, a rollover, shifted mounting points, intruded parts, sustained casing heat above 60 C, or water inside the pack. Those packs are NOT tested further and must be disposed of. The user's brief says "escalation"; the document says "excluded from closer testing, must be disposed of". The German VDA/ZDK guideline (Jan 2026) and TUV-Verband whitepaper (May 2026) cover transport, quarantine and the test types (insulation resistance, thermography, vehicle data), but I found no numbers in them. Insurers' own technical arm (Allianz AZT) and Thatcham say the central problem is the lack of OEM-independent battery data and repair instructions: with no data, a scratched pack whose cells are probably fine gets written off (Reuters, Mar 2023). Frequency is low but cost is high: in an AZT sample, battery damage was 2% of 400 BEV collision claims but about 7% of claims cost; replacement cost EUR 13,300-43,300; casing swap EUR 1,100-2,200 (AZT, Jan 2023, small sample). Quarantine is long and ad hoc: Thatcham cites a UK 15 m storage rule and salvage yards holding EVs about a week; AZT says VW and BMW cut initial quarantine to 24 h with temperature monitoring (Aug 2026); a Swedish fire officer cites two weeks and 10 m (not an official rule). Critical view of what an assessment can detect: it reliably finds gross mechanical damage, water ingress, fire or heat exposure, open fault codes, insulation faults and large cell-voltage or temperature deviations that the BMS reports. It cannot reliably prove that an apparently intact pack is safe. SVV itself says a battery can have thermal, mechanical, electrical or chemical stress that is "possibly not visible from outside" and then has an "undefined state". TUV SUD says internal damage may not be visible. Fraunhofer's X-ray (AIR, about 10 min per vehicle) can show shifted or swollen cells, but it is research or pilot stage (more than 100 private cars scanned in 2024), no price or insurer customer is published, and in the ID.3 case images alone did not clear the pack: DEKRA hazard evaluation, EDR/BMS data and electrical tests were also needed. A latent defect that shows up weeks later (NHTSA's 2011 Volt test: fire 21 days after the crash test) is not ruled out by any one-time check. Vendors: I found NO vendor with a published post-crash battery assessment price for insurers. AVILOO, DEKRA and TWAICE products found are SoH or residual-value tests, not post-crash safety assessment. Tractable, Ravin, CCC, Mitchell and Audatex are photo or estimating tools with no evidence of battery-damage models. For the pitch, the credible gap is "OEM-independent, insurer-accepted evidence that lets a claims handler avoid or shorten quarantine and avoid a premature write-off", not "we detect battery damage". Insurer acceptance (liability if a cleared pack later burns) is the main hurdle (Reuters quote from repair-shop owner).

items.topic: Swiss SVV/ASS/LiBaService24 annex: the test procedure and exclusion thresholds (primary)
items.finding: Annex 'Umgang mit beschädigten Hochvolt-Fahrzeugbatterien' to the ASS BTVE guideline, v9, initiated by the SVV expert committee and LiBaService24 (members include Baloise, Allianz Suisse, Zurich). Signed 31 Oct 2025; file metadata 27 Feb 2026; posted on svv.ch 2026-03. Test is explicitly non-destructive. Two stages: (1) hazard analysis at the scene or parking place (decides transport with or without fire-protection system and whether quarantine is needed; HV1+HV2 training minimum); (2) function analysis in a workshop with a lift: documents (police report, handover report, BTVE event 4-8), physical impact (rollover, shift of the pack at mounting points, intruding parts), visual check (underbody and casing dents/cracks/holes, cooling plates and leaks, water ingress, heat above 60 C, soot, extinguishing agent, airbag and belt-pretensioner deployment, all connectors and bolts), electrical/electronic analysis (fault memory, BMS data: SoC, individual cell voltages, module voltages, module temperatures, cell voltage difference, communication with all modules and temperature sensors, insulation values, SoH, OBD, pyrofuse status). Work on live HV parts needs HV3. Status outcome: functional / repairable / damaged-defective / significantly damaged-critical. EXCLUSION (no further testing, must be disposed of): multiple rollover; significant shift at mounting points; foreign object penetrating the pack; casing deformation >=10 mm deep or torn casing or holes; sustained external heat >60 C at the casing; event 8 (cells/modules involved in fire); water in the pack. The guide states its thresholds are averages from OEM data and literature and the OEM's instructions always prevail, and that no exhaustive procedure can be given because of the variety of packs. NOTE: the 10 mm figure is an exclusion/disposal trigger, not just an 'escalation' trigger. Costs are not given for the test itself; the annex only covers extra disposal costs for significantly damaged packs (ChemRRV).

items.topic: Allianz Center for Technology (AZT): how often batteries are damaged and what it costs
items.finding: AZT analysed a random sample of 400 Allianz BEV comprehensive-collision claims from 2021 (350 ICE comparison cases). HV battery damaged in 2% of cases, those 2% caused about 7% of total claims cost. Five underbody cases needed full battery replacement (battery cost EUR 13,300-43,300), three more were saved by replacing the casing (EUR 1,100-2,200; cheapest EUR 1,100 by only swapping the underbody shield). Only one intrusion case. Mean BEV claim 18% above ICE, median 6% above. Report notes small case numbers. In insurance law the injured party is owed restoration of the original condition, so even cosmetic casing damage can force a large-part replacement because casing repairs are not approved. AZT position paper (14 Dec 2023): some OEM rules require battery replacement after any pyrotechnic (airbag/belt tensioner) deployment; replacement cost 'approx. 10,000 to over 40,000 euros'; AZT says the crash load cannot be derived from airbag triggering; for some OEMs there are no clear mechanical or electronic criteria to evaluate the pack; an OEM OK/not-OK battery status is insufficient; AZT asks for standardised data access, 3D design data and replaceable casing parts; expects 6,000-11,000 battery-damage claims in Germany in 2030 (AZT estimate). Aug 2026 AZT interview: battery damage costs range from under EUR 1,000 up to EUR 29,000; brand workshops about 50% higher hourly rates; manufacturer tools usually tell reliably whether a battery is faulty, independent workshops often lack the diagnostic scope; AZT asks for a value-adjusted replacement battery to avoid total loss.

items.topic: Thatcham Research (UK): EV Blueprint, diagnostics gap, quarantine
items.finding: Thatcham/Cebr survey: battery issues are the top concern for 44.6% of insurers and 41.7% of repair professionals. March 2026 'EV Blueprint': 8 recommendations incl. clear post-crash battery damage assessment methods available to all (incl. independent repairers and insurers), standardised HV diagnostics on widely available equipment (not proprietary subscription tools), casing/bracket repair without removing the pack, and a proposed dedicated British Standard (BSI project page exists) on HV battery damage assessment and repair. Thatcham says current OEM methods mostly support full casing replacement with little validated repair guidance; example: 3-year-old EV with minor side impact on the battery bracket becomes a write-off. Earlier Thatcham research (2023): UK government guidance says damaged EVs awaiting repair should be stored outdoors at least 15 m from other objects, so a yard for 100 ICE cars holds only about 2 EVs; Thatcham's Adrian Watson: 'diagnostics we have do not enable you to really know' battery status; salvage plants quarantine EVs about a week. I did not find a Thatcham 'category' scheme specific to battery damage (UK write-off categories A/B/S/N exist generally but I found no battery-specific categorisation). Counter-evidence: CAP HPI says EVs are written off far less often than ICE cars in Britain.

items.topic: German-language guidance: VDA/ZDK guideline, TUV-Verband whitepaper, TUV SUD
items.finding: VDA-led cross-industry guideline (Jan 2026, with ZDK): requirements for transport, interim storage and quarantine of potentially damaged HV batteries; free; does not replace training. I could not retrieve its numeric rules (distances, hours). TUV-Verband whitepaper 'Bewertung verunfallter Hochvoltbatterien in Elektrofahrzeugen' (reported 6 and 11 May 2026): battery must be examined systematically, tests named: insulation resistance, thermography, evaluation of vehicle data; internal short circuits and thermal instability can develop with a delay; module repair is often much cheaper than whole-pack replacement; decision depends on SoH and vehicle replacement value; no numeric thresholds, costs or quarantine durations were published in the coverage. TUV SUD / VW dealer damage manager (AUTOHAUS 7 Sep 2026): visible damage often appears only at considerable force; an externally inconspicuous pack does not rule out internal damage; about 30% of crashed vehicles reaching his dealership are hybrids and about 10% pure EVs. Third party regional example: a ZKF/Audi slide cites 5 m clearance on a paved quarantine area; self-ignition possible after several days.

items.topic: Delayed thermal runaway: time windows, distances, observation
items.finding: No single harmonised European time window found. Sources conflict: UK 15 m storage; NTSB/NFPA/NHTSA US 50 ft (about 15 m) clearance; Swiss AGVS: critical batteries outdoors, observed, safety container; one German fire-association figure reported by AUTOHAUS: 72 h observation after extinguishing, while ingenieur.de reports at least 24 h with stable battery temperature below 80 C (secondary reports, not verified against the fire-service originals); VW/BMW cut initial quarantine to 24 h with temperature monitoring (AZT, Aug 2026). Swedish fire officer (SVT) cites two weeks and 10 m (practitioner statement, not MSB). Re-ignition days to months is stated in NTSB and US first-responder material; NHTSA's 2011 Chevy Volt side-pole test: fire 21 days later. Water immersion: German GDV says severely damaged EVs are often held in quarantine or sunk in extinguishing containers, which often leads to total loss; Allianz AU says OEMs do not recommend submerging; Idaho National Lab documents immersion tanks for flood-damaged packs. Not found: gas-sensor or thermal-camera protocols with numeric thresholds, and quarantine cost per day.

items.topic: Fraunhofer AIR X-ray: what it can and cannot do
items.finding: Fraunhofer IIS with Munich UAS: AIR (Antriebsbatterieinspektion mittels Röntgentechnik), drive-through X-ray of whole vehicles, about 10 min per vehicle; new 2026 software auto-detects cell type (cylindrical, prismatic, pouch) and flags displacement, deformation, swelling; about 5 min automated evaluation per pack in the test environment. Pilot (2024) with more than 100 private cars. On a crash-damaged ID.3 the pack was rated EUCAR 0 but X-ray alone did not justify reuse; DEKRA hazard evaluation, EDR and BMS data and electrical tests were also used. A second pack with cylindrical cells showed no swelling but strongly deformed zone and displaced cells; reuse advised against. Fraunhofer says it is not meant to replace electrical tests. A VW e-Up crashed at 50 km/h had massive front damage but the X-ray showed the HV storage intact. No price, no insurer customer, no announced deployment. Lab/few locations worldwide for full-vehicle inspection per Fraunhofer. A separate Fraunhofer 'Giant Eye' CT in Fürth is planned. INNER (CT scanner for packs) found; no insurer acceptance evidence found. Critically: it sees geometry, not electrolyte decomposition, lithium plating, internal short circuits or latent separator damage.

items.topic: Repair vs replace vs total loss: how the decision is taken and what drives it
items.finding: Decision is made by the insurer's claims handler/expert on repair cost vs vehicle value, with OEM instructions deciding whether casing repair or module exchange is allowed. Many OEMs allow only whole-pack or casing replacement; Tesla reportedly replaces packs whole (secondary sources, no Tesla manual found). Reuters (20 Mar 2023): Allianz has seen scratched packs with likely undamaged cells but must write off without diagnostic data; UK salvage firm Synetiq estimated at least 95% of cells in stored EV packs undamaged and reusable (company estimate); repair-shop owner: insurers will not take the later-lawsuit risk. German GDV (24 Jul 2024, 38 model series): EV comprehensive claims 20% fewer but 25% more expensive each; quarantine/extinguishing containers often lead to total loss. A frequently cited 'GDV 30-35% higher repair cost' appears in the AZT paper (2023) and a Austrian press report. Dutch rule of thumb (Unive): repair above EUR 7,000 = economic total loss (one insurer, not a standard). Norwegian TU (older) says some insurers total above 60% of new-car value (single secondary statement). CCC (US, 2025 data): 12.7% of EV claims were total losses vs 23.1% for all vehicles, i.e. EVs are NOT written off more often overall; the problem is concentrated in battery-involved claims. Nordic dispute practice (FinKN, Norway): insurers must document, and fault arising after the event does not by itself prove the event caused it.

items.topic: Cost and duration of the checks themselves (weakly sourced)
items.finding: No official price list for a post-crash HV battery check was found. One AI-assisted German blog (elektronik-zeit.de, updated 11 Oct 2026; self-declares AI assistance, many claims unsourced) gives: 'HV diagnosis Lite' (BMS read-out + insulation test) EUR 150-300, 1-2 h; 'Full' (capacity analysis over controlled cycle) 2-3 working days; it lists what such diagnostics miss: micro-deformation of the tray without visible marks, detached module connectors or internal sensor cables, insulation damage that only appears in humidity, cooling-loop damage that shows at the next fast-charge, and a clean generic OBD2 scan does not confirm HV health. Treat as low-confidence. German article: after a crash both a body expert report and a workshop HV diagnostic protocol are needed; for minor damage the injured party may carry the expert cost. SoH tests for used cars (not post-crash): ADAC/ecomento-type guide EUR 100-150; AVILOO Premium test EUR 99 consumer, OeAMTC Flash test EUR 69. DEKRA 15-minute battery test is a capacity check. In Riga (user's own data) EUR 60-130.

items.topic: Vendors and services: who offers post-crash battery assessment
items.finding: No vendor found with a productised, priced post-crash battery assessment sold to insurers. AVILOO: SoH test/certificate and battery warranty (expanded to 26 countries Sep 2026; Intec bundle Jun 2026); partners ADAC NRW, GTU, OeAMTC; no insurer post-crash cooperation found. TWAICE: battery analytics with insurance-backed accuracy guarantee (Munich Re's Great Lakes); partnership with broker NARDAC (2024) is for stationary storage; no post-crash vehicle product found. Volytica (Fraunhofer spin-off): analytics for storage and fleets, Mahle charge-plug diagnostics project (2022); no post-crash service found. DEKRA: 15 min capacity test for used EVs; DEKRA Netherlands damage expertise investigates cause and extent of damage for insurers (no price); DEKRA does hazard evaluations for Fraunhofer cases. TUV SUD offers SoH diagnosis. Tractable: photo-based total-loss triage, 95-98% claimed accuracy (2020 interview), 20+ insurers; no battery model found. Ravin: insurer capture, total-loss triage (vendor positioning via a competitor blog). CCC/Mitchell/Audatex(Solera): estimating platforms; no validated battery-damage model found. Werksta Sverige and a Nordic 'only workshop of its kind' (TU, Jul 2026, paywalled) repair batteries. LiBaService24 (Swiss, co-author of the SVV annex) offers analysis/transport of damaged packs: no prices found. Not found: Cartesian, Allianz/AZT outsourced service. Salvage: Synetiq (IAA/RB Global) runs isolation bays and resells packs (UK); Copart procedures not found.

Sweden: TV4 (Apr 2023): small damage can scrap an EV because many OEMs do not allow battery repair; Konsumenternas: insurers differ in compensation (20/50/100% of new-battery cost after 5 years); I did not find If or Trafikforsakring procedures. Netherlands: AutoRAI (Reuters-based) says battery damage can quickly mean economic total loss; an independent expert decides; no Dutch national post-crash battery guideline found. Latvia: nothing found on Balta/BTA/ERGO EV battery assessment; ERGO terms refer to the LTAB-approved vehicle technical expertise methodology for residual value and total loss; Ayvens notes the pack is part of the platform in most EVs.

checks.claim: Swiss SVV/ASS annex v9 (signed 31 Oct 2025): casing deformation >=10 mm deep, torn casing/holes, >60 C sustained heat, multiple rollover, shifted mounts, foreign object -> excluded from closer testing and must be disposed
checks.note: I read the PDF text. Section 7.1: these packs 'are excluded from closer testing ... must be disposed of without closer testing'. Signed 'Saland, 31. Oktober 2025', Version 9; PDF metadata 27 Feb 2026. Nuance: the 10 mm, 60 C, rollover, mount-shift and foreign-object items sit in the 'beschaedigt/defekt' table. 'Event 8' and 'water in the battery' sit in the 'erheblich beschaedigt/kritisch defekt (must be disposed)' table. The document also says thresholds are averages and OEM instructions prevail. It is a voluntary industry guideline (section 2 'rechtlicher Stellenwert'), not law. The brief's 'escalation' wording is wrong; the researcher's correction is right. Note WebFetch summarised this PDF wrongly (returned a Shiptec title), so rely on the raw text. Also check that the title metadata does not belong to a different document.

checks.claim: AZT/Allianz sample: battery damaged in 2% of 400 BEV collision claims (2021) but about 7% of claims cost
checks.note: Confirmed on the AZT page and in the AZT PDF (random sample of 400 Vollkasko collision claims from 2021, quota 2% of claims, 'gut 7%' of cost). Critical caveat: 2% of 400 is about 8 cases, so the 7% cost share is statistically very weak. The PDF itself says case numbers are small. The AZT PDF also says it verified against the whole 2021 claims base, which the researcher did not mention. Allianz Germany's separate '8% of claims costs' comes from Reuters (Mar 2023) and is a different basis.

About 5 min is automated evaluation time in the test environment. X-ray does not assess SoH or electrochemical state. Note the ID.3 was a lab crash, not a real-world claim. Research stage.

The source is a vendor report (CCC sells claims software). US data, so weak for Latvia. Also this says EVs are written off less often overall, which undercuts a 'too many write-offs' pitch.

checks.claim: Thatcham/Cebr survey: battery issues are top concern for 44.6% of insurers and 41.7% of repair professionals; EV Blueprint (Mar 2026) asks for clear battery damage assessment guidelines and standard HV diagnostics
checks.note: Repairer Driven News 5 Mar 2026 confirms both figures and the 8 recommendations (assessment guidelines for all incl. independent repairers and insurers; standard HV diagnostics on common equipment). Question wording and survey date are not given. Thatcham is insurer-funded lobbying research. The demand for standards supports the problem but also means a standard is likely to be set by Thatcham/BSI/OEMs, not a start-up.

checks.claim: NHTSA 2011 Chevy Volt: fire 21 days after crash test
checks.note: NHTSA document text: 'Twenty-one days after the May 12, 2011 testing, delayed thermal heating and pressure release resulted in a fire'. Caveat: this was a lab side-pole test followed by vehicle rotation with coolant loss, a worst-case protocol, and is a 2011 single vehicle. It is not a base rate. The researcher correctly notes that no frequency of delayed runaway was found.

checks.claim: Reuters Mar 2023: Allianz writes off scratched packs with likely good cells for lack of data; Synetiq says at least 95% of cells in stored packs undamaged; repair-shop owner says insurers fear later lawsuit; Allianz battery damage 8% of Germany claims costs
checks.note: Confirmed via the devdiscourse repost of Reuters. The 95% is a company estimate by a salvage firm (it has a commercial interest) and applies to packs in its yard, not to crash-scratched packs. The lawsuit-fear quote is one repair-shop owner (Peter Gruber), not an insurer. The 8% is an Allianz Germany statement that differs from AZT's 7%. These are 3.5-year-old statements.

checks.claim: Post-crash HV diagnosis 'Lite' costs EUR 150-300 and takes 1-2 h; 'Full' takes 2-3 working days
checks.note: Article exists and gives these numbers, but it discloses AI-assisted drafting and cites no source for the prices or durations (its cited sources are DGUV, DEKRA 2019, NHTSA TSBs, Reuters). Treat as an unverified estimate and do not use it as a price anchor in the pitch. No primary or vendor price for a post-crash check was found in my searches either.

corrections: The AZT cost ranges (EUR 13,300-43,300 and 1,100-2,200) are not on the cited HTML page; they are in the AZT PDF 'Analyse Kollisionsschaeden HV Fzge'. Cite the PDF URL. The HTML page gives only the 2% / 7% / 400 / 2021 data.
The AZT '2%' means about 8 battery cases out of 400 (5 replacements, 3 casing swaps). Report n=8 next to any '7% of cost' number. Data is 2021 claims, published Jan 2023, so prices are dated.

SVV annex: the brief's 'escalation' is wrong, and the researcher is right. But the 10 mm / 60 C / rollover items are formally in the 'beschaedigt/defekt' table and only 'event 8' and 'water in battery' are headed 'must be disposed'. The intro text still says all excluded packs 'must be disposed of without closer testing'. The guideline is voluntary and says OEM instructions prevail. Do not present 10 mm as a legal or insurer rule.
CCC's 12.7% vs 23.1% is a vendor statistic with no stated definition, US-only. Label it vendor/US.
The Synetiq 95% is a salvage company estimate for packs in its yard. Do not use it as evidence that crash-scratched packs are fine.
Fraunhofer's 'EUCAR 0, cleared' result was a lab crash test of one ID.3 at DEKRA, not a field claim. Do not present it as proof of diagnostic capability.
The NHTSA 21-day fire was a worst-case lab protocol (post-crash rotation, coolant loss) on one 2011 vehicle. It shows possibility, not frequency.

The AZT interview says manufacturer diagnostic tools 'generally give good information' on whether a battery is defective. The researcher's summary stresses the lack of OEM-independent data and under-weights this. The real gap is independent workshops, the scene or storage decision, and OEM rules that mandate replacement, not absence of any diagnostic.
The elektronik-zeit.de EUR 150-300 figure is an AI-assisted blog with no cited source for prices. It should not be cited as a market price.
missed: VW 'Bewertungskatalog HV-Batterie' (AUTOHAUS, 16 Jan 2023, presented at the Allianz Autotag): an OEM-issued assessment catalogue for MEB batteries distributed to dealers, workshops, experts and insurers. AZT's Lauterwasser says it can save about EUR 10,000-30,000 per case by avoiding full HV unit replacement. This is direct competition or substitution risk: OEMs are producing their own post-crash criteria and bypass any third-party scanner. It is also the only quantified saving per case I found (trade press, one AZT quote).

AX report (UK, late 2025; am-online / fleetworld) says no standardised post-crash diagnostic and quarantine procedures exist and urges national standards. I could not fetch the full text (403). It corroborates the gap and shows it is a standards-setting fight.

Reuters/Tesla: Sandy Munro called the Model Y structural pack 'zero repairability'. For structural-pack vehicles, an assessment cannot change a replace-or-repair outcome, which limits the addressable savings.

AZT position paper (14 Dec 2023) says crash load cannot be derived from airbag triggering and that some OEMs mandate battery replacement after pyrotechnic deployment. A third-party assessment may not override OEM rules, so insurer savings depend on OEM acceptance, not on detection accuracy.

GDV says severe damage cases with quarantine or extinguishing containers often become total losses. The strongest insurer-cost argument is therefore quarantine and logistics cost and time, not the measurement itself, and I found no per-day quarantine cost anywhere.

No evidence was found of any insurer paying a third party for a post-crash battery scan; my own search found only calls for standards and no launches. Absence of buyers is a finding the pitch must address.
Not verified in this pass: UK 15 m storage rule, Swedish and Dutch claims, VDA/ZDK and TUV-Verband documents, and the Latvian market. The 24 h/72 h quarantine figures remain secondary reports.

findings.angle: B: insurer economics for EV claims (frequency/severity, total loss, battery share of claim cost, towing/storage/quarantine, fire, salvage, repair-first, published triage savings)
findings.summary: The strongest hard data on the weak point of the post-crash-scan thesis comes from Allianz's AZT: in a 400-claim EV sample the battery was involved in only about 2% of collision claims (about 7% of claim money). Total-loss rates for EVs are roughly the same as for comparable combustion cars (Mitchell, CCC) or lower (Cap HPI, UK). So a battery-focused scan helps in a small share of claims, but those claims are expensive (battery repair EUR <1,000 up to EUR 29,000; pack GBP 14,200-29,500). The clearer money pools are (a) avoiding unnecessary write-offs when the damage is only casing/bracket (Thatcham blueprint, Mar 2026, but no quantified savings), (b) towing/quarantine/storage costs (Allianz: towing about double in 2025, up to EUR 19,217 for one claim; Spiegel case over EUR 20,000), and (c) fire/quarantine decisions, where hard frequency data show EV fires are not more common than ICE (MSB, GDV). Critical findings: no published case study or pilot with measured insurer savings from post-crash battery triage was found; a Thatcham official said (2023) that current diagnostics do not give a full picture of battery status, so a scan cannot yet reliably certify hidden cell damage; Latvian/Baltic EV claim data and Norwegian/Swedish salvage price data were not found; there is no clean salvage price percentage for damaged EVs. Sources are mostly trade press secondary reports; several figures are US/Canada (Mitchell/CCC) and not transferable to Latvia.

items.finding: Allianz Center for Technology (AZT) sample of 400 EV collision claims: HV battery involved in only 2% of cases but about 7% of total claim amount because of high unit cost. Brand workshops charge almost 50% higher hourly rates than independents. An earlier AZT analysis found about 18% higher Vollkasko collision damage for EVs (EVs much younger than comparison cars). Reported by trade press, 19 Aug 2026 and 10 Aug 2026 (interview with AZT researcher). I could not extract text from the AZT PDF itself (compressed), so these are secondary reports of AZT data.

items.topic: Total-loss rates EV vs ICE
items.finding: Evidence is mixed and does not support 'EVs are written off far more often' at population level. Mitchell (US/Canada) Q1-Q3 2023: EV 7.25% vs all ICE 8.49%, but Mitchell states the Li-ion battery significantly raises total-loss likelihood once damaged. Mitchell Q1 2024: EV 9.93% US / 7.48% Canada vs newer ICE 9.51% / 7.44%; rise attributed to falling used-EV values. CCC: 12.7% of EV claims were total losses in 2025 (up almost 2 pts) vs 23.1% industry-wide. Mitchell Q1 2026: BEV 12% vs new ICE (<6 yrs) 13%. UK Cap HPI (data to Aug 2024): under-5-year-old EVs written off 0.9% vs 1.89% for petrol/diesel. Opposing UK estimate by FWD Consulting (Dec 2025): about one in five collided EVs written off, more than GBP 461m a year cost to businesses; methodology not verified, consultancy source. Key insight: total loss is driven by vehicle value (falling used-EV prices) as much as by battery damage.

items.topic: Battery damage leading to unnecessary write-off; what the Thatcham EV Blueprint says
items.finding: Thatcham EV Blueprint (published 4-5 Mar 2026; 8 recommendations) says current mandated procedures frequently produce total losses because casing/bracket damage can require a new battery costing more than the car is worth; example is a 3-year-old EV written off for a minor side impact that damaged a battery bracket. Preferred route: repair casing without removing the pack; fallback: cheaper refurbished unit; calls for modular construction, bolted not bonded fixings, resettable pyro fuses, and HV diagnostics accessible to independent repairers and insurers. It gives no quantified savings. Thatcham 2023 (via press): diagnostics available do not really tell the battery status; one press summary also quoted 'underbody damage is 85% likely to result in battery damage' but I could not verify that in the fetched source, so treat as unconfirmed. Generational tested 8,000+ EVs: median state of health 93.53% for 4-5-year-olds and 85% for 8-9-year-olds. Dutch/Reuters-based reporting (Mar 2023) said some insurers total a car for a small scratch on the pack.

items.topic: Towing, quarantine and storage costs of crashed EVs
items.finding: Allianz (Germany) found 2025 EV towing costs averaged almost exactly double those of conventional vehicles; highest single Allianz claim EUR 19,217. A Spiegel case: Peugeot e-208 towing invoice over EUR 20,000 (pre-transport consultation about EUR 1,700, battery removal and storage box EUR 2,450 net, battery expert EUR 1,650). VDA/GDV/ADAC and 20+ associations issued a joint guideline (Dec 2025) to cut excessive quarantine; VW and BMW cut initial quarantine to 24 hours with battery temperature monitoring. A wildlife-collision case: storage fee about EUR 1,300 plus more than EUR 100/day (Jan 2026). A court (LG Koblenz) reduced a towing firm's EUR 38,569.81 claim for a hybrid (incl. EUR 95/day quarantine) to EUR 7,596.96 storage, with 76.16/day for first five days then 19.04/day; the liability insurer had already paid EUR 5,459.01. GDV says water-container sinking regularly causes total loss; a 2018 fire-brigade example cites about EUR 70,000 for a quench container. This is a distinct, better-documented insurer cost pool than battery replacement itself, and it is addressable by a fast, trustworthy risk triage.

items.topic: Published savings from better triage/assessment
items.finding: Searched in English, German, Dutch, Swedish and Latvian: no insurer announcement, pilot or case study with measured savings from post-crash battery assessment was found. items.topic: Critical assessment: what a post-crash assessment can and cannot detect
items.finding: Can: structural/casing deformation and underbody impact (visual, thermography), insulation resistance faults, BMS fault codes and SoH from vehicle data, and shock-load history if a sensor exists. Cannot (per sources): Thatcham head of engineering research said diagnostics available 'do not enable you to really know' battery status and current capability falls short of a complete picture (2023); invisible internal cell damage can lead to delayed fire (Danish SKAD); German press recommends specialised tests because damage is not visible from outside. Also: manufacturer repair procedures can mandate pack replacement regardless of a third-party scan, and AZT says costs are largely driven by manufacturer norms; the battery is involved in only about 2% of claims, so a scan product earns on a small, high-value subset. The insurer buyer needs OEM acceptance and liability cover for a 'safe to repair/store' verdict. These are analysis notes combining the cited sources, not measured results.

LG Koblenz: EUR 7,596.96 is the total storage fee awarded (and EUR 5,459.01 already paid), not an additional amount; the remainder was much smaller than claimed (about EUR 2,138 if only that payment was made). Case is a (plug-in) hybrid, first instance, Az. 14 O 169/24, judgment 4 May 2026. Source type is legal press (LTO, DATEV Magazin), not the judgment text.

CCC '12.7% vs 23.1%' should not be used as a like-for-like comparison: 23.1% is an undefined 'overall industry total loss rate' (all ages), so it overstates the ICE comparator. The like-for-like Mitchell numbers (12% vs 13%, Q1 2026) are the better evidence.
Cap HPI 0.9% vs 1.89% covers data from 2015 to August 2024, UK, under-5-year-old vehicles; not a 2024 snapshot. Cap HPI is a vendor, not an official statistic.

The Thatcham 'diagnostics do not enable you to really know' statement is better read as a lack of OEM data access plus immature tools: Reuters-based coverage says Allianz writes off scratched packs because it lacks manufacturer diagnostic data. That supports a data/access angle for a scan product, but also means a third-party scan may not be accepted by OEM repair procedures.
The 'official' label on the DATEV item in the researcher's table is wrong (legal trade press). MSB 40/38 fires were verified only via Vi Bilagare, not MSB's own publication.
GDV '14,200 car fires in 2023' was not found in the Autohaus article; unverified.
missed: The researcher did not date the AZT sample: the real base is small (about 8 battery cases in 400) so the key 'battery in only 2% of claims' stat has a very wide confidence interval and may reflect 2021-era EVs. Any pitch should say 'low single-digit % of EV collision claims, high cost each' and not cite exactly 2%/7%.

Dependence on OEM repair procedures: Thatcham's own example (battery bracket/casing damage mandates new battery) shows the insurer's lever is the OEM repair rule, not information. A scan only saves money if the insurer or repairer can deviate (Thatcham calls for this, but it is a recommendation, not a rule), or if the scan certificate is accepted by OEMs/liability bodies.

Court practice limits the paid-quarantine pool: LG Koblenz capped quarantine rates to 5 days and used normal parking rates thereafter; VW and BMW cut the initial quarantine to 24 hours with battery temperature monitoring (firmenauto, 10 Aug 2026), and a joint VDA/GDV/ADAC guideline (reported by the researcher, Dec 2025) targets excessive quarantine. The addressable savings from quarantine are therefore shrinking even before a scan, and the Allianz doubling (2025) reflects a transitional period.

Mitchell states that once the battery is damaged, total loss likelihood is significantly higher; CCC shows EV values -46% since Oct 2022. Together: total loss is driven by low used-EV values, so for older/cheap EVs the scan cannot rescue the car economically (repair > value either way), narrowing the segment (young, high-value EVs).

Mitchell BEV share of claims is only 3.33% (US) / 4.94% (Canada) in Q1 2026, and German EV share is 3.3% of cars; the number of post-crash EV events a Latvian insurer faces per year is small (no Latvian claim data found by either researcher). Data points that point at a different buyer or value route: Allianz UK GBP 50,000 average lithium-battery fire claim (all lithium, Nov 2024) is not EV-car specific and was kept as 'official' by the researcher; it was not re-verified here.
No independent source found for the claim that scan certificates raise salvage prices; the salvage uplift part of the thesis is still an assumption.

Not re-checked in this pass: the Dutch/AutoRAI (2023) light-battery-damage total-loss item, Norwegian write-off thresholds (60-80% of value, undated Bytt.no), the Dagens PS +40%, and the Allianz Cornhill recycled-parts analogy (undated, old); all remain weak, undated, or analogical.

findings.angle: C: competitors and adjacent services selling to insurers/loss adjusters (AI estimating, EV battery diagnostics, salvage/quarantine, mobile inspection), pricing models, funding, evidence of savings, failures, Baltic coverage
findings.summary: Nobody found sells a post-crash, battery-health-specific assessment to insurers on a per-assessment price or subscription. The market splits into four non-overlapping layers. (1) Photo/AI damage estimating (Tractable, CCC, Solera/Audatex, Ravin, Claim Genius) is sold to insurers, but it sees exterior damage and has no documented high-voltage battery capability. (2) EV battery diagnostics (AVILOO, TWAICE, Volytica, Generational) are sold to dealers, auctions, leasing, fleets and BESS owners; insurers appear as a named audience or reinsurance backer (Munich Re/Great Lakes for TWAICE), not as a documented paying customer for post-crash assessment. (3) Salvage/storage players (Copart UK, German hazard-management firms) sell quarantine and handling, with no published prices. (4) Inspectors and experts (TÜV SÜD, TÜV-Verband, DEKRA, AZT, Thatcham) set methods and guidance; the TÜV-Verband whitepaper (Sept 2026) and the SVV guideline (Feb/Mar 2026) are standards, not a priced product. The pain is documented and primary-sourced: Thatcham (Mar 2026) says battery issues are the top concern for 44.6% of insurers; AZT says battery damage costs range from under EUR 1,000 to up to EUR 29,000 and that quarantine is often excessively long, and the sample of 400 collision damages showed only 2% involved the battery. That last point is a critical limit on the business case: the battery is rarely the damaged part, so volume of paying events may be small. Thatcham explicitly warns against subscription-based proprietary diagnostic tools and wants open, cheap HV diagnostics on common equipment, which pressures price and favours OEM/open tools. No Baltic coverage found for any player: AVILOO's insurer-backed warranty covers 24 European countries and explicitly excludes Latvia, Estonia, Lithuania; Copart has no Baltic yards (Finland is nearest); Audatex Baltics UAB exists in Vilnius (9 staff per an AI-generated registry page, low confidence); no Latvian insurer (BTA, ERGO, Balta, Gjensidige) source on EV battery claims handling was found. Failure/lessons evidence is thin: no shutdowns or layoffs found in 2025-26 searches; the one dependency risk is that evidence of savings is mostly vendor claims or targets, not audited. Reference price points: Ravin enterprise AWS listing USD 84,000 per year for up to 20,000 inspections (about USD 4.20 per inspection, own calculation); manufacturer-level battery SoH reading in Latvia EUR 30-80 (guide, not an insurer price). Opening for a new entrant: independent, brand-agnostic, post-crash decision support plus safe storage/routing in a region with none of the incumbents, but it must prove detection value and cost savings with a pilot, since no competitor publishes any.

items.topic: Honest limits of a post-crash assessment (critical view)
items.finding: Evidence in the sources: (a) Detectable: BMS fault codes and logs, SoH, insulation resistance, thermal anomalies, voltage/temperature behaviour, visible casing deformation (SVV treats 10 mm or more as grounds for escalation, per the team's brief). (b) Not reliably detectable: internal cell damage or latent defects from an outwardly intact pack (TUV SUD states an unremarkable exterior does not rule out damage); delayed thermal events can emerge hours or days later (Copart/Thatcham-reported); SoH tests such as AVILOO FLASH measure capacity, not mechanical integrity. Hence no one sells a guarantee of 'no fire risk'; AVILOO's insurer-backed product covers accelerated degradation only. Also, manufacturers can mandate replacement after airbag deployment regardless of measured health, so an independent scan may not change the outcome unless OEM procedures allow it. Combine with the 2 percent battery-involvement sample (AZT) and a smaller addressable volume than headline EV claims suggest.

findings.angle: D: Baltic and Latvian market (insurers, claims, EV crash/fire data, ELV/salvage rules)
findings.summary: The Latvian motor-insurance market is small and concentrated, but no source I found gives Baltic EV-specific claims data (EV share of CASCO claims, EV total losses, EV crash counts, battery-related claim cost). Hard numbers exist only for the whole market: 2025 CASCO premiums EUR 138m, 2024 CASCO claims about EUR 86m, 2025 OCTA 35,617 claims averaging EUR 1,762. The EV stock is about 13,000 cars (1.6% of the fleet, Oct 2025, secondary source), so EV crashes are likely a few hundred a year at most. That figure is my own inference, not a sourced number. Latvian insurers (via LAA) say the EV premium gap has closed and that a separate battery deductible may apply. The only quantified EV crash-cost material is Estonian and Nordic press, and it is anecdotal. Hard numbers on EV fires and post-crash fires in the Baltics are missing; Latvian VUGD publishes totals (523 vehicle fires in 2025) with no EV split, and its public advice is generic. The LAA chief says burned cars are mostly old diesels. Latvia has no published rule I could find on assessing, quarantining or storing crashed EV batteries, and the ELV rules (MK 135, MK 896) I found do not address EV traction batteries. A Latvian per-claim volume case for a post-crash scan therefore cannot be built from public data. It would need insurer data, which implies early interviews with 2-3 insurers (BTA, Balta, If, ERGO, Compensa, Gjensidige) and the LTAB/LAA. Critically, the Latvian OCTA/CASCO data suggest the typical claim is small (EUR 1.7k average OCTA), so most EV crashes never come near the battery, and the value sits in the rare high-severity underbody and airbag cases.

items.topic: Critical read: what this means for the idea in Latvia
items.finding: (1) Latvia's insurer market is concentrated, but I found no named EV claims owner or procurement signal; the first step is customer discovery with insurer claims heads. (2) Volume is thin: about 13k EVs, OCTA average claim EUR 1,762, 35.6k OCTA claims a year across all cars; EV claims where battery is in doubt are a small subset. (3) The Nordic evidence suggests the money is in the tail: airbag or underbody hits where manufacturer rules force pack replacement (EUR 15k to 85k). A scan helps only if it can show the pack is fine (avoid replacement) or confirm damage early; casing deformation of 10 mm is an escalation threshold, not a health result. (4) Many Baltic EVs are used imports from Germany and Scandinavia with unknown pack history, and insurer practice may be to follow the manufacturer's dealer diagnostic, which an independent scan does not replace; the dealer's decision is likely binding for warranty and liability. (5) EV fire risk after a crash in Latvia is not evidenced: officials describe EV fires as rare; the VDA concern is over-caution, not fires. A scan could cut quarantine and tow-off costs, but that benefit is unproven locally.

findings.angle: E: legal, safety, data and link to battery chain (post-crash scan sold to insurers)
findings.summary: Bottom line: nothing legally stops a third party from issuing a post-crash battery assessment, but nothing in the law gives that assessment special standing either. The gate is access (HV-qualified people, OEM data, a quarantine site) plus credibility with insurers, not a licence. (1) Latvia has no battery-specific licence. A general regime exists: Cabinet Regulation No. 251 of 2005 certifies technical experts for vehicle damage and loss assessment. Per likumi.lv it is in force but lapses 1 July 2027, so check what replaces it. ISO/IEC 17020 inspection-body accreditation (LATAK in Latvia) is voluntary but is the obvious credibility route. Note: the 2026 edition collapses Type A/B/C into Type A and Type non-A, and a firm that also sells battery-chain services would not be Type A. (2) What an assessment can really detect: the 2025-26 German sources (TÜV-Verband whitepaper, May and Sept 2026) say external condition does not show internal damage, and name insulation resistance, thermography and vehicle-data evaluation as the methods. A thermal event means full pack replacement. The decision is often still made by the manufacturer or a specialist workshop per manufacturer specs. So a third-party scan can triage and document, but sources do not show it can replace OEM release; that is the main weakness of the pitch. (3) Data: a lawful owner has read access to BMS state-of-health data, including independent operators and waste managers, under Art. 14(2) Reg. 2023/1542 (applies from 18 Aug 2024). Delegated Reg. 2026/699 (in force 23 June 2026) extends OEM repair information to battery diagnostics and safe handling, but OEMs may require tool/operator authentication. The Data Act (applies from 12 Sept 2025) lets the user route data to a third party, but the Commission guidance is non-binding and only 'where relevant and technically feasible'. Crash-specific GDPR rules were not found. (4) Transport and storage: SP 376 and P908 are confirmed via secondary sources; P911/critically defective was found via BAM and vendor pages only, and the ADR 2025 official text was not retrieved. German VDA recommendation (Dec 2025) says damaged EVs are generally handled like ICE cars unless real battery damage is suspected, with temperature-monitored quarantine of 'one to a few days'. Others cite up to 72 hours and 15 m clearance; these are not harmonised. (5) Ownership and routing: could not verify the user's GRS tariffs (EUR 1.44/kg NMC, 4.38/kg LFP); GRS public price lists show container deposits and 'on request' pricing instead. Thatcham's EV Blueprint (3 Mar 2026) explicitly calls for open battery-damage assessment methods for insurers and independent repairers, and BSI has a proposed standard on HV battery damage assessment. This is strong market validation, but it is a voluntary industry call and no formal standard or grade scheme was found.

items.finding: ADR SP 376 covers damaged/defective Li-ion cells and batteries, marking 'DAMAGED/DEFECTIVE' and a transport-document statement; P908 is the packing instruction; critically defective batteries are tied to P911/LP906 and BAM rules per German sources (ADR 2025 reportedly adds a new special provision, number reported as SV 677, which I could not confirm; official text not retrieved). UN note (2018): damaged/defective is judged by safety criteria from the manufacturer or a technical expert. VDA (Dec 2025): damaged EVs are moved to the nearest suitable site (usually a specialist workshop); interim parking only exceptionally; quarantine, if hazard suspected, with temperature monitoring, ended after one to a few days without temperature rise depending on OEM spec. The 15 m clearance is cited by UK press (attributed to Thatcham, unconfirmed), by Australian NT fire service and a Florida FAQ; NHTSA's interim guide says 50 ft. UK Environment Agency draft waste standards also mention a 15 m radius. Insurer-specific salvage yard requirements from Allianz/AXA/Zurich: not found. ABI Salvage Code updated May 2025 to include EVs.

items.topic: Battery damage grades and Thatcham
items.finding: The ABI Salvage Code categories (A scrap, B break, S structural repairable, N non-structural repairable) are vehicle-level, not battery-level; no battery damage grade is defined in them per search results. Thatcham's EV Blueprint (3 March 2026, eight recommendations) calls in Rec. 3 for clear battery damage assessment methods open to independent repairers and insurers, and Rec. 4 for standardised, widely available HV diagnostics. Battery up to 40 percent of vehicle value. Battery issues are the top concern for 44.6 percent of insurers and 41.7 percent of repair professionals (Thatcham/CEBR survey). BSI project proposes a British Standard for HV battery damage assessment and repair, because BS10125 only gives broad guidance. No finished grading standard exists; this is an opening for a third-party grade, but also means insurers have no accepted grade to buy yet. A grade would need to map to OEM release decisions to be actionable.

synthesis.verdict:
VERDICT (31 Oct 2026): Insurers will probably not pay for a standalone "post-crash battery scan" in Latvia today. They might pay for a faster, defensible decision on a small number of expensive EV claims. Right now the evidence supports a pilot hypothesis, not a proven product.

What insurers would be paying for, in order of how well the evidence supports it:
1. Shorter or avoided tow, battery-removal and quarantine cost. Allianz says EV towing cost about double that of conventional cars in 2025, with a top claim of EUR 19,217 (trade press, auto-motor-und-sport, 4 Mar 2026). VDA says tow firms often remove HV batteries from fear of fire even after minor damage (AUTOHAUS, 14 Jan 2026). This is the best-documented cost pool, but it is shrinking. VW and BMW cut initial quarantine to 24 h with temperature monitoring (AZT, firmenauto, 10 Aug 2026). A German court capped daily storage rates (LG Koblenz, a plug-in hybrid, first instance, May 2026).
2. Avoiding a premature write-off or full pack swap when only the casing or bracket is hit. Thatcham's EV Blueprint (Mar 2026) gives the example of a 3-year-old EV written off after minor bracket damage. It quantifies no savings. AZT found 3 of about 8 battery cases in its sample were solved with a casing swap of EUR 1,100-2,200 instead of a EUR 13,300-43,300 pack.
3. Evidence they can show a regulator, a claimant or a court. This is the weakest point. A third-party scan cannot override OEM repair rules. AZT says some OEMs mandate replacement after airbag or pyrotechnic deployment, and an insurer owes restoration of the original condition.

Why not yet:
- Volume is tiny. AZT found the battery involved in about 2% of EV collision claims (n=400, about 8 cases, reportedly 2021 claims) but about 7% of claim cost. Latvia has about 13,000-13,900 EVs. My own estimate is about 57 triggered assessments per year market-wide (see value estimate). That is not a business by itself.
- Nobody pays for this yet. Across all four research angles I found no insurer pilot, tender or case study with measured savings from post-crash battery assessment, and no vendor selling one at a published price. This is either an open gap or a signal of weak demand, and we cannot tell which from desk research.
- Detection is limited. See the detect/cannot-detect section.
- OEM-independent data is the insurers' actual complaint (Allianz, Thatcham, GDV). The likely winners are OEMs (VW's assessment catalogue for MEB packs), standards bodies (Thatcham/BSI, SVV, TUV-Verband, VDA) and the incumbent experts (DEKRA, TUV, AZT), not a start-up.

What would convince an insurer:
(a) a retrospective review of their own EV claim files showing where a scan would have changed a decision;
(b) the scan agreeing with the OEM dealer diagnostic in parallel testing;
(c) zero false "all clear" verdicts on packs that later fail;
(d) turnaround within 24 h of the tow;
(e) liability cover for a "safe to store or repair" verdict;
(f) a price below the value of one avoided day of quarantine plus a small share of an avoided pack swap.

Recommended framing for the pitch: do not sell "a scan". Sell a post-crash decision and handling service for damaged EV packs. It has three parts: triage to the SVV-style criteria, safe storage and routing, then repair, second life or recycling through our chain. The scan is the entry gate. Revenue comes from handling and routing, not from the scan fee. Present all savings as hypotheses to be tested in a pilot.

Date corrections for the team brief: the SVV annex is signed 31 Oct 2025 (v9) and was posted in March 2026. The brief says Feb 2026. The 10 mm casing figure is an exclusion-and-disposal trigger, not an "escalation" trigger.
how_post_crash_assessment_works_today: Stage 1, scene and tow: police or rescue services secure the car. A tow firm, often without a standard rule, decides on transport (with or without a fire-protection container) and whether the pack is removed. The Swiss SVV/LiBaService24 annex (v9, signed 31 Oct 2025, posted Mar 2026, [official but voluntary guideline]) calls this the hazard analysis, with HV1 plus HV2 training as the minimum. URL: https://svv.ch/sites/default/files/media/documents/2026-03/202600227_Anhang%20Leitfaden_HV-Batterie%20Analyse_DE.pdf

Stage 2, workshop function analysis on a lift (SVV annex): review documents (police report, event type 4-8); check physical impact (rollover, shifted mounting points, intruding parts); visual check of underbody and casing (dents, cracks, holes, cooling plates and leaks, water ingress, heat above 60 C, soot, extinguishing agent, airbag and belt-pretensioner deployment, connectors and bolts); electrical read-out (fault memory, SoC, cell and module voltages and temperatures, cell voltage difference, insulation values, SoH, pyrofuse status). Live HV work needs HV3. Outcome is one of four classes: functional, repairable, damaged/defective, significantly damaged/critical. The test is non-destructive.

SVV exclusion rules (no further testing, dispose): casing deformation 10 mm or more deep, torn casing or holes, sustained casing heat above 60 C, multiple rollover, significant shift at mounting points, foreign object penetrating the pack, cells involved in fire, water in the pack. The guide states its thresholds are averages from OEM data and literature, and that OEM instructions always prevail. Strictly, only 'event 8' and water-in-pack sit in the 'must be disposed' table. The others sit in the 'damaged/defective' table, though the intro text still says excluded packs are disposed of without closer testing (skeptic check of the PDF text).

Germany: a VDA-led industry guideline with ZDK (Jan 2026, free) covers transport, interim storage and quarantine. The TUV-Verband whitepaper (reported 6-11 May 2026 and 7 Sep 2026) names insulation resistance, thermography, vehicle data and fault logs, and a cost-benefit test against replacement value. I found no numeric thresholds in the press coverage and could not retrieve the full documents. [trade press summaries]

Insurer or expert decision: a claims handler or expert compares repair cost with vehicle value. OEM rules decide whether casing repair or module exchange is allowed. Many OEMs allow only whole-pack or casing replacement (AZT position paper 14 Dec 2023). Allianz has seen scratched packs with probably undamaged cells that were written off for lack of OEM diagnostic data (Reuters via devdiscourse, 20 Mar 2023).

Quarantine practice has no harmonised standard. UK: 15 m separation for damaged EVs awaiting repair (Thatcham/Innovate UK coverage, 2023). US: 50 ft (NTSB, collisionweek 14 Jan 2021). Swiss AGVS: critical packs outdoors, observed, in a safety container (4 Mar 2026). Germany: the fire-association observation period is reported as 72 h in one place and at least 24 h in another, both secondary. VW and BMW use 24 h plus temperature monitoring (AZT, 10 Aug 2026). A Swedish fire officer cited two weeks and 10 m (SVT, practitioner statement, not a rule).

Duration and price of the checks: not found as an official or vendor price. One AI-assisted German blog (elektronik-zeit.de, 11 Oct 2026) says EUR 150-300 and 1-2 h for a 'Lite' diagnosis, and 2-3 working days for a 'Full' one. The skeptic flagged it as unsourced, so do not use it as a price anchor. [low confidence]

AZT says manufacturer tools usually tell reliably whether a battery is faulty. The hard parts are the on-site assessment, where to park safely, and the fact that independent workshops often lack the diagnostic scope (firmenauto.de, 10 Aug 2026, trade press). So the gap is OEM-independent access and the scene and storage decision, not the absence of any diagnostic.

Latvia: I found no published Latvian procedure, insurer statement or VUGD guideline for assessing or quarantining crashed EV batteries. ERGO's CASCO terms define total loss only as repair that is technically impossible or economically unjustified. LTAB certifies OCTA experts and keeps the loss-assessment methodology. [searched, not found]
what_an_assessment_can_and_cannot_detect: CAN detect reliably: gross mechanical damage (casing dents measured in mm, cracks, holes, shifted mounts); water ingress; fire or heat exposure; open BMS fault codes; insulation faults; large cell-voltage or temperature deviations that the BMS reports; pyrofuse and airbag status; a fast-moving temperature rise during an observation period. Sources: SVV annex 2025/26 [official]; TUV-Verband, AUTOHAUS and ecomento May and Sep 2026 [trade press].

CAN detect with caveats: SoH and capacity (AVILOO, DEKRA 15-minute test, TWAICE) measure capacity, not mechanical integrity. They do not show a cracked cell housing or a latent separator defect. Thermography and X-ray show geometry and heat, not electrochemical state.

CANNOT reliably prove an apparently intact pack is safe. SVV itself says a pack can carry thermal, mechanical, electrical or chemical stress that is possibly not visible from outside, and that it then has an 'undefined state'. TUV SUD says an unremarkable exterior does not rule out damage. TUV-Verband says internal short circuits and thermal instability can develop with a delay. [official / trade press]

CANNOT rule out delayed events with a one-time check. NHTSA's 2011 Chevrolet Volt test ended in a fire 21 days after the crash test (NHTSA document INOA-PE11037). The skeptic notes this was a worst-case lab protocol with post-crash rotation and coolant loss, on one vehicle, so it shows possibility, not frequency. I found no source for the share of crashed EVs that suffer delayed thermal runaway. [not found]

Fraunhofer AIR X-ray (about 10 min per vehicle, more than 100 cars in the 2024 pilot, 2026 software that flags displaced or swollen cells) is research-stage. It has no published price and no insurer customer. In the ID.3 lab crash case the pack was rated EUCAR 0, yet X-ray alone did not justify reuse. DEKRA hazard evaluation, EDR and BMS data, and electrical tests were also needed (electrive, 22 Sep 2026). Fraunhofer says it does not replace electrical tests.

CANNOT change an outcome that OEM rules fix. If the OEM mandates pack replacement after airbag deployment or the pack is structural (the Tesla Model Y 'zero repairability' remark attributed to Sandy Munro, secondary), a third-party scan has no decision value. Insurer savings depend on OEM or liability-body acceptance, not on detection accuracy (AZT 14 Dec 2023: crash load cannot be derived from airbag triggering).
CANNOT see inside the pack with drive-through camera scanners (UVeye type). They see the exterior and underside only.

Known blind spots of simple diagnostics, from the low-confidence German blog (11 Oct 2026): micro-deformation of the tray with no visible marks, detached module connectors or internal sensor cables, insulation damage that only shows in humidity, and cooling-loop damage that shows at the next fast-charge. A clean generic OBD2 scan does not confirm HV health. Treat as plausible but unverified.

Net for the pitch: the defensible claim is 'faster, documented triage that finds gross damage and flags uncertain packs for quarantine or disposal'. It is not 'we detect battery damage' and not 'we certify a pack as safe'.

where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.cost_driver: Full battery replacement in the tail of underbody and impact claims
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.evidence_and_numbers: AZT/Allianz sample of 400 EV Vollkasko collision claims (reportedly 2021 claims, published Jan 2023): HV battery involved in 2% of claims (about 8 cases) but about 7% of claim cost. Five cases needed a new pack at EUR 13,300-43,300; three more were saved with a casing swap at EUR 1,100-2,200. The n=8 means very wide uncertainty and the prices are 2021. where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.could_an_assessment_reduce_it: Only if OEM rules allow deviation. Thatcham's own recommendation is for standards and repairable designs, not for a start-up scan. High value in theory, low controllability.

where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.cost_driver: Towing, battery removal and special transport
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.evidence_and_numbers: Allianz: 2025 EV towing costs about double those of conventional vehicles; highest single Allianz claim EUR 19,217. A Spiegel case (Peugeot e-208): towing invoice over EUR 20,000, including EUR 2,450 net for battery removal and storage box and EUR 1,650 for a battery expert (auto-motor-und-sport.de, 4 Mar 2026) [trade press]. The doubling is a ratio, and I found no absolute average cost per EV tow.
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.could_an_assessment_reduce_it: Yes, if a fast on-scene or early triage prevents unnecessary pack removal and container transport. This is the best-supported pool, but the cases cited are outliers and the practice is already being corrected by the VDA/GDV/ADAC guideline (Dec 2025 / Jan 2026).

where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.evidence_and_numbers: Thatcham 2023: a 48 h quarantine adds at least GBP 60 per claim and a yard for 100 ICE cars holds about 2 quarantined EVs (insurance-edge.net 5 Jul 2023, trade press). Harz case: storage fee about EUR 1,300 plus more than EUR 100 per further day (firmenauto.de, 21 Jan 2026). LG Koblenz (Az. 14 O 169/24, 4 May 2026, a plug-in hybrid, first instance): a tow firm claimed EUR 38,569.81 including EUR 95/day quarantine; the court awarded EUR 7,596.96 in total storage at EUR 76.16/day for 5 days then EUR 19.04/day. The EUR 7,596.96 is the total, not an extra amount (LTO 4 Jun 2026; DATEV Magazin 16 Jun 2026) [legal press].
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.could_an_assessment_reduce_it: Yes, by cutting quarantine days. The pool is shrinking (OEM 24 h rule, court caps), so treat it as modest per claim.

where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.cost_driver: Higher general EV claim severity (not battery-specific)
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.evidence_and_numbers: GDV (Aug 2025, 53 EV model-series pairs): Vollkasko severity about +15-20% vs comparable combustion cars, frequency about -10-15% (autohaus.de 18 Aug 2025, trade press). Thatcham 2023: BEV claims about +25.5% and 14% slower to repair. Mitchell Q1 2026 (US): repairable severity BEV USD 6,042 vs ICE USD 4,902 [vendor / trade press]. Repair-cost gap is converging (CCC: EV vs hybrid gap USD 1,809 in 2020 to USD 445 in 2025 for 7+ year old vehicles).
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.could_an_assessment_reduce_it: Mostly no. This is parts and labour, not battery assessment. It shows EVs cost more, but the cost is spread across many claims.

where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.evidence_and_numbers: EVs are NOT written off more often overall. Mitchell Q1 2026: BEV 12% vs new ICE 13% (repairerdrivennews.com, 21 May 2026). Cap HPI UK (data 2015 to Aug 2024): under-5-year-old EVs 0.9% vs 1.89% petrol/diesel [vendor]. Do NOT use CCC's 12.7% vs 23.1%: the 23.1% is an all-age, undefined-denominator industry rate. Opposing estimate: FWD Consulting (Dec 2025) says about 1 in 5 collided EVs are written off, methodology not verified. Drivers: falling used-EV values (CCC: EV values -46% since Oct 2022) as much as battery damage. Mitchell notes that once the battery is damaged, total-loss likelihood rises significantly.
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.could_an_assessment_reduce_it: Only for young, high-value EVs where repair is feasible. For older, cheap EVs, repair exceeds value either way.

where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.evidence_and_numbers: Sweden MSB: 40 fires in electric/hybrid passenger cars in 2024 (38 in 2023), verified only via Vi Bilagare. GDV: about 13,600 insured car fires in 2024 with about EUR 100m paid, all drivetrains, and no evidence EVs burn more. Latvia VUGD: 523 vehicle fires in 2025 (397 passenger cars), with no EV split; LAA chief says about 90% of burned cars are older than 5 years and about 90% diesel [official / trade press]. Frequency of delayed post-crash re-ignition and cost per EV fire: not found. Allianz UK average lithium-battery fire claim GBP 50,000 covers all lithium types, not EV cars.
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.could_an_assessment_reduce_it: Narrative value is high, expected-loss value is not supported by frequency data. Do not lead the pitch with fire.

where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.evidence_and_numbers: AZT: brand workshops charge almost 50% higher hourly rates; independent workshops often lack the diagnostic scope (firmenauto.de, 10 Aug 2026). Estonia: labour about EUR 70/h (up to 90) vs EUR 160-190 at Finnish Tesla service (ERR 14 Feb 2024).
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.could_an_assessment_reduce_it: Possibly, by enabling independent repair decisions. Unquantified.

where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.cost_driver: Salvage and residual value of damaged EVs and packs
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.evidence_and_numbers: No usable figure found for damaged-EV auction price as a share of pre-loss value (Copart, IAA, BCA, Autoplius, Norwegian and Swedish salvage all searched). Synetiq (UK salvage, company estimate) says at least 95% of cells in stored packs are undamaged, but that is a salvage firm's estimate for packs in its yard, not crash-scratched packs (Reuters via devdiscourse, 20 Mar 2023). Allianz 2023: capacity loss of up to 20% can cut resale value by up to 25%.
where_insurers_lose_money_on_evs.could_an_assessment_reduce_it: Plausibly (a scan certificate supports a buyer's confidence), but no data show the uplift. Treat as an assumption to test.

synthesis.value_per_assessment_estimate: ["BASELINE FRAME: value per ASSESSED claim = (probability the scan changes a costly decision) x (cost avoided) + (quarantine and tow days avoided) x (cost per day). Nothing here is measured. The sourced inputs are marked [S], my assumptions [A]. If an assumption is wrong, the answer moves a lot.", "INPUT 1 [S]: battery involved in about 2% of EV collision claims, n=400, about 8 cases, reportedly 2021 (AZT, Jan 2023). Replacement EUR 13,300-43,300 (5 cases); casing swap EUR 1,100-2,200 (3 cases). [A] Trigger rule (airbag fired, underbody impact, casing contact, towed from scene) flags 10% of EV collision claims. Then about 20% of assessed claims have real battery involvement (2% / 10%), assuming the trigger catches every real case. If the trigger catches only half, precision is 10%.", "INPUT 2 [A]: in a real battery case, the scan (with OEM or insurer acceptance) changes the outcome from full pack replacement or write-off to a casing or module repair in 15% of cases (low 5%, high 25%). There is no source for this share. It is the single most important unknown. AZT's 3-in-8 casing-swap cases happened without a scan, so they are not incremental.", "INPUT 3 [A + S range]: net saving when the outcome changes = EUR 8,000 (low EUR 6,000, high EUR 15,000). Basis: AZT replacement from EUR 13,300, minus an assumed EUR 2,000 repair, minus a haircut for cars where the repair costs more or the OEM refuses. AZT's EUR 1,100-2,200 casing swap and its EUR 29,000 upper range bracket this.", "CENTRAL CASE, battery-decision component: 0.20 x 0.15 x EUR 8,000 = EUR 240 per assessed claim. Low: 0.10 x 0.05 x EUR 6,000 = EUR 30. High: 0.30 x 0.25 x EUR 15,000 = EUR 1,125.", "INPUT 4 [S range + A]: quarantine and tow. Sourced daily rates: EUR 76.16/day for days 1-5 then EUR 19.04/day (LG Koblenz award), more than EUR 100/day (Harz case), EUR 95/day (claimed in Koblenz), and GBP 60 per 48 h (Thatcham 2023). [A] The scan shortens or avoids quarantine by 3 days on 50% of assessed claims, at EUR 50/day: 0.5 x 3 x 50 = EUR 75 (low: 1 day x 30% x EUR 30 = about EUR 10; high: 5 days x 70% x EUR 100 = EUR 350). Battery removal and container transport avoided (Spiegel case EUR 2,450 net) in an assumed 5% of assessed claims: about EUR 120 (low 0, high EUR 250). The Spiegel item is a single anecdote.", "CENTRAL TOTAL: about EUR 240 + 75 + 120 = about EUR 435 gross savings per assessed claim. Low about EUR 40. High about EUR 1,700. I set aside fire loss (no frequency data), salvage uplift (no data) and goodwill or claim-speed benefits as zero.", "COST SIDE [A]: the insurer already pays for some diagnostic today (Riga SoH test EUR 60-130, team data; low-confidence blog EUR 150-300). Our delivery cost for a mobile HV visit (technician 2-3 h, tools, travel, insurance) is an assumption of EUR 120-200 per assessment. So at a price of EUR 150-200 the insurer's central net gain is about EUR 235-285 per assessed claim, but in the low case the insurer loses money and our margin is near zero.", "VOLUME CHECK [S + own estimate]: Latvia had about 12,991 EVs on 1 Oct 2025 (1.6% of cars; LSM 26 Oct 2025, secondary) and the team uses about 13,900 at end 2025. LTAB reports 35,617 road accidents reported to insurers in 2025 (LTAB release 15 Jan 2026, official). If EVs are involved proportionally, about 1.6% x 35,617 = about 570 EV accidents a year (own estimate, ignoring that EVs have fewer claims per GDV and that the LTAB count is accidents, not vehicles). At a 10% trigger that is about 57 assessments a year across ALL Latvian insurers, worth about EUR 25,000 of gross savings in the central case. Baltics-wide, with Estonia at 7,834 electric-drive vehicles (Nov 2024) and Lithuania at an undated and unverified 28,000, the figure is perhaps 200-300 assessments per year. This is a few tens of thousands of euros of revenue, which is a service line, not a company. Volume grows with the EV fleet but not fast enough to carry the venture alone.", "SANITY CHECK: 2% x EUR 13,300-43,300 on an EV claims base also implies that the total money in battery claims is small in Latvia. The market only becomes meaningful in Germany or the Nordics, where competitors and standards bodies are already active. We have no moat there."]
